title: 第7章 冰融第8章 山中漫步
content_zh:
三天过去了。
三天里，帐篷顶上那六个补丁——三个大的、三个小的——她数了不止一百遍。
有时候是醒着的时候数的，有时候是半梦半醒的时候数的。数着数着就睡着了，数着数着又醒了。醒来之后再从头数，数完六个再从头数。
她不知道自己为什么要数。
数补丁有什么用？什么都改变不了。
但她还是数。
因为她需要数点什么。
如果什么都不数，脑子里就会空下来。空下来就会想。想了就会疼。疼了就会哭。哭了就很软弱很软弱，软弱到她自己都看不起自己。
她不想哭。
她已经很久没有哭过了。
所以她数补丁。一个、两个、三个、四个、五个、六个。数完了再从头数。
数到后来，她已经不记得自己是第几遍了。
张老头每天来三次。早上一次，中午一次，晚上一次。
来做什么她不知道，也不想知道。她只知道他进来的时候会掀开帐帘，会端一碗粥，会在她手腕上按一会儿，然后说一些她不想听的话。
“脉象稳了些。“
“再养两天。“
“这丫头，就是不开口。“
她不答。
张老头也不追问。
他只是把粥放在她床边的小几上，然后转身出去。

她不看他。
她只看着帐篷顶。
张老头走的时候，帐帘会掀开。帐帘掀开的时候，外面的声音会传进来。
有时候是马蹄声，踏踏踏踏的。有时候是号角声，呜呜的，很长。有时候是人的说话声，嘻嘻哈哈的，很远，听不清在说什么。
她听着那些声音，听着听着，就把眼睛闭上了。
不是因为困。
是因为不想听。
外面的世界太吵了，吵得她心烦。她已经习惯安静了，习惯了一个人待在山里，听着风声、水声、树叶沙沙响。那些声音是干净的，干净的像水。
营地的声音不干净。
那些声音里有人。有人的笑，有人的喊，有人的吵。
她不想听人的声音。
第二天下午，帐外忽然传来一阵笑声。
笑声很清脆，脆得像银铃。是女人的笑声。
“小盈，你来啦！“
“来啦！但不是找你，是找肖大哥的。“
“我还不稀罕找你呢！哼！“
那女人的声音嗔嗔的，带着点娇。另一个声音是男的，跟着起哄。
“唉，我说你俩能不能消停会！每天都斗嘴！“
她躺在帐篷里，听着那些声音。
那些声音很远，远得像是另一个世界。

她闭上眼睛，把头埋进枕头里。
枕头是软的，软得把声音都捂住了。
但她还是能听见。
content_en:
Three days passed.
In three days, she counted the six patches on the roof of the tent—three large and three small—more than a hundred times.
Sometimes I count while I'm awake, sometimes I count while I'm half asleep. I fell asleep while counting, and woke up again after counting. After you wake up, count from the beginning again. After counting six, count from the beginning again.
She didn't know why she was counting.
What's the use of counting patches? Nothing can be changed.
But she still counts.
Because she needed something to count.
If you don't count anything, your mind will be empty. I will think about it when I have free time. It hurts just thinking about it. I cry when it hurts. Crying makes her very weak, so weak that she even looks down on herself.
She didn't want to cry.
She hadn't cried in a long time.
So she counts patches. One, two, three, four, five, six. After counting, count from the beginning again.
By the end of the count, she couldn't remember how many times she had done it.
Old man Zhang comes here three times a day. Once in the morning, once at noon and once in the evening.
She didn't know what she was doing, and she didn't want to know. She only knew that when he came in, he would open the curtain, bring a bowl of porridge, press his hand on her wrist for a while, and then say something she didn't want to hear.
"The pulse is more stable."
"Take another two days."
"This girl just won't speak."
She didn't answer.
Old man Zhang didn't ask further questions.
He just put the porridge on the small table beside her bed, then turned and went out.
She didn't look at him.
She looked only at the roof of the tent.
When old man Zhang leaves, the curtain will be opened. When the curtain is opened, sounds from outside will come in.
Sometimes it’s the sound of horse hooves, tapping, tapping, tapping. Sometimes it's a horn sound, whining, very long. Sometimes it’s the sound of people talking, laughing and joking, but it’s so far away that you can’t hear clearly what they are saying.
She closed her eyes as she listened to those sounds.
Not because of sleepiness.
It's because I don't want to hear it.
The world outside was too noisy and it made her upset. She was used to being quiet, used to being alone in the mountains, listening to the sound of wind, water, and rustling leaves. Those sounds are clean, as clean as water.
The sound of the camp is not clean.
There was someone in those voices. Some people laugh, some people shout, and some people make noises.
She didn't want to hear human voices.
The next afternoon, a burst of laughter suddenly came from outside the tent.
The laughter was very clear, as crisp as a silver bell. It's a woman's laughter.
"Xiaoying, you're here!"
"Here we come! But I'm not looking for you, I'm looking for Brother Xiao."
"I'm not looking for you! Humph!"
The woman's voice was angry and a little coquettish. Another voice, male, followed.
"Oh, I asked you two to stop for a while! We bicker every day!"
She lay in the tent and listened to the sounds.
Those sounds were far away, like another world.
She closed her eyes and buried her head into the pillow.
The pillow was soft, so soft that it muffled the sound.
But she could still hear it.
